main.title: NiGHTS into Dreams...
main.subtitle: Flight through an analogue controller
main.summary: On July 5, 1996 Sega released NiGHTS into Dreams... for Saturn in Japan.

cards.heading: Sonic Team takes flight
cards.text: On July 5, 1996 Sega released NiGHTS into Dreams... for Saturn in Japan. Sonic Team imagined a game in which the character flies through three-dimensional spaces while control remains readable, built around trajectories, rings, paraloops and scoring. The 3D analog controller, also sold in a bundle, makes the curve of movement part of the experience. Flight follows defined routes through these spaces, letting players concentrate on smooth curves, linked actions and scores.

cards.heading: Flight, the Drill Dash and linking
cards.text: NiGHTS flies along a set route, with a timer limiting how long the transformation lasts. Collisions remove precious seconds, while returning an Ideya replenishes them. The Drill Dash accelerates flight and attacks enemies; a complete loop joins the star trail and pulls nearby items inward. Collecting objects and passing through rings in quick succession builds a Link, rewarding a flowing route rather than isolated actions. Speed, timing and the shape of the flight therefore become parts of the same scoring decision.

cards.heading: Designing the Saturn analogue controller
cards.text: The development took longer than expected because of the team's inexperience with Saturn hardware and uncertainty about using the full 560 megabyte space on the CD-ROM. They initially thought the game would consume around 100 megabytes of data, and at one point considered releasing it on two discs. Iizuka said that the most difficult part of development was handling the "contradiction" of using 2D sidescroller controls in a fully 3D game. Naka limited the flying mechanic to "invisible 2D tracks" because early beta testing revealed that the game was too difficult in full 3D. The standard Saturn gamepad was found to be insufficient to control Nights in flight, so the team developed the Saturn analog controller. It took about six months to develop, and the team went through many ideas for alternate controllers, including one shaped like a Nights doll.

cards.heading: Grades, bosses and split-screen competition
cards.text: The player receives a grade based on their score at the end of each Mare, and an overall grade for the level after clearing all four Mares. Nights is then transported to Nightmare for a boss fight against one of Wizeman's "Level Two" Nightmarens. Each boss fight has a time limit, and the game ends if the player runs out of time during the battle. Upon winning the boss fight, the player is awarded a score multiplier based on how quickly the boss was defeated, which is then applied to the score earned in the Nightopia section to produce the player's final score for that Dream. In the multiplayer mode, two players battle in splitscreen. One player controls Nights, whereas the other controls Reala. The winner is the first player to hit or paraloop the other three times.

main.title: Saturn Bomberman
main.subtitle: A roomful of rivals
main.summary: Saturn Bomberman is Hudson Soft's maze action game, first released for Saturn in Japan on 19 July 1996.

cards.heading: A roomful of rivals
cards.text: Saturn Bomberman is Hudson Soft's maze action game, first released for Saturn in Japan on 19 July 1996. Players place bombs in a grid of corridors, break soft blocks and try to catch opponents in the resulting explosions. Its most famous feature expands that familiar contest to ten players through multitap accessories. The larger gathering makes the arena a place of rapidly changing threats, where a bomb placed elsewhere can close an escape before the player has finished dealing with the danger immediately in front of them.

cards.heading: A bomb changes the maze
cards.text: Bombs send fire along the maze's open lines, so choosing where to place one also means preserving a route away from it. Breaking blocks reveals more space and useful power-ups, changing the possibilities as a round continues. Dinosaur helpers hatch from eggs and can be ridden, providing special abilities and absorbing a hit for their rider. They grow through further collection, with the battle mode using additional eggs for that growth. The helper gives a vulnerable player another chance, but a crowded arena can consume that protection almost immediately.

cards.heading: More than the battle arena
cards.text: Alongside competitive play, a story mode provides a sequence of stages, while Master mode asks the player to finish challenges quickly and records a rank. These modes let the same bomb placement support exploration, survival and measured performance. Jun Chikuma composed the soundtrack, maintaining the series' bright, energetic atmosphere. The ten-player battles remain the defining attraction because they magnify a remarkably clear rule: every player understands what a bomb will do, yet several people acting at once can turn a readable corridor into a trap in seconds.

main.title: Tobal No. 1
main.subtitle: A fighting game with room to step aside
main.summary: Tobal No. 1 is DreamFactory's PlayStation fighting game, first released in Japan on 2 August 1996. Characters designed by Akira Toriyama compete in three-dimensional arenas, where movement around the opponent is part of the exchange. The player chooses between high, middle and low attacks, then mixes strikes with grappling and defence. Its uncluttered character designs keep those actions readable as the fighters circle one another. The game brings together an experienced fighting-game designer and an artist strongly associated with manga, giving Square an unusual entry into a genre outside its best-known role-playing games.

cards.heading: A fighting game with room to step aside
cards.text: Tobal No. 1 is DreamFactory's PlayStation fighting game, first released in Japan on 2 August 1996. Characters designed by Akira Toriyama compete in three-dimensional arenas, where movement around the opponent is part of the exchange. The player chooses between high, middle and low attacks, then mixes strikes with grappling and defence. Its uncluttered character designs keep those actions readable as the fighters circle one another. The game brings together an experienced fighting-game designer and an artist strongly associated with manga, giving Square an unusual entry into a genre outside its best-known role-playing games.

cards.heading: Get close enough to change the contest
cards.text: The ability to move through the arena makes distance and angle matter alongside the next attack. Closing in can turn an exchange of strikes into a grapple, where the relationship between the two bodies becomes the central problem. The player has to read the opponent's response and decide whether to continue the pressure or move away. Quest mode takes the fighting system into dungeon exploration, giving those same controls another purpose beyond a conventional tournament. A system learned against one rival becomes a way to navigate a longer sequence of encounters.

cards.heading: A notable team behind an unusual Square game
cards.text: Seiichi Ishii directed the game after contributing to Virtua Fighter and Tekken, while Toriyama supplied its cast. A large group of Square composers worked on the soundtrack, including Yasunori Mitsuda, Yoko Shimomura and Masashi Hamauzu. Japanese and North American copies also included a sampler disc with a playable Final Fantasy VII preview, giving the release another place in PlayStation history. Tobal itself received a generally positive response and found particular success in Japan. Its sequel remained Japan-only, leaving the original as the series' principal international release.

main.title: Dark Savior
main.subtitle: A prisoner on the loose
main.summary: Dark Savior is Climax Entertainment's adventure, first released for Saturn in Japan on 30 August 1996.

cards.heading: A prisoner on the loose
cards.text: Dark Savior is Climax Entertainment's adventure, first released for Saturn in Japan on 30 August 1996. Bounty hunter Garian is escorting the dangerous creature Bilan to a prison island when it escapes aboard the ship. His pursuit begins a story whose direction depends on how quickly he reaches the captain's cabin. Exploration uses an angled three-dimensional view, with platforming and puzzles between conversations. Fights then move into a separate side-view system. These changes make the journey a sequence of different tasks, connected by Garian's investigation and the consequences of his opening pursuit.

cards.heading: Changing the rules of an encounter
cards.text: Exploring the island requires judging jumps and finding a useful view around obstacles. The camera can be adjusted to reveal routes hidden by the scenery, while combat confines the characters to a two-dimensional plane despite its three-dimensional presentation. Certain defeated opponents can be captured and used in later fights, adding another reason to learn their abilities. Items found during exploration can also be traded for information, other objects or points. Those points support practical choices, including improving Garian's health or helping him recover from a defeat.

cards.heading: One arrival, several possibilities
cards.text: The time taken during the shipboard opening determines which parallel story follows. Returning to the beginning can therefore lead into another version of the adventure, where events and encounters develop differently. That structure makes an action performed before the player fully understands its importance into the hinge of the whole journey. Climax had previously made Landstalker, and the angled exploration recalls that experience, but Dark Savior adds its own divided narrative and separate fighting system. The result asks the player to learn both the island's spaces and the possibilities concealed in an earlier arrival.

main.title: Crash Bandicoot
main.summary: Crash Bandicoot is a 1996 platform game developed by Naughty Dog and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation.

cards.heading: A platform game with several viewpoints
cards.text: Crash Bandicoot is a 1996 platform game developed by Naughty Dog and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation. The player controls Crash, a genetically enhanced bandicoot created by the mad scientist Doctor Neo Cortex. The story follows Crash as he aims to foil Cortex's plans for world domination and rescue his girlfriend Tawna, a female bandicoot also created by Cortex. The game is played from a third-person perspective in which the camera trails behind Crash, though some levels feature forward-scrolling and side-scrolling perspectives.

cards.heading: From a road trip to a PlayStation character
cards.text: After accepting a publishing deal from Universal Interactive Studios, Naughty Dog co-founders Andy Gavin and Jason Rubin set out on a cross-country road trip from Boston to Los Angeles. During this time, they decided to create a character-based action-platform game from a three-dimensional perspective, having observed the graphical trend in arcade games. Upon meeting, Naughty Dog and Universal Interactive chose to develop the game for the PlayStation due to Sony's lack of a mascot character. The game's main character was tentatively named "Willy the Wombat", and cartoonists Joe Pearson and Charles Zembillas were hired to help create the game's characters and story. Crash Bandicoot was named for his habitual destruction of crates, which were inserted into the game to alleviate emptiness in the levels. Sony agreed to publish the game following a demonstration from Naughty Dog, and the game was unveiled at E3 1996.

cards.heading: Different audiences, different versions
cards.text: Crash Bandicoot was released to generally positive reviews from critics, who praised the game's graphics, presentation, audio, difficulty level and title character, but criticized its linearity and lack of innovation as a platform game. The game went on to sell over 6 million units, making it one of the best-selling PlayStation games with particularly strong sales in the United States. For the game's Japanese release, the gameplay and aesthetics underwent extensive retooling to make the game more palatable for Japanese audiences, and as a result it achieved commercial success in Japan. Crash Bandicoot became the first installment in an eponymous series of games that would achieve critical and commercial success and establish Naughty Dog's reputation in the video game industry. A remake was released as a part of the Crash Bandicoot N. Sane Trilogy in 2017.

cards.heading: Moving into the screen
cards.text: Crash Bandicoot is a platform game in which the player controls the titular character Crash, who is tasked with traversing 32 levels to defeat Doctor Neo Cortex and rescue Tawna. Most of the game takes place from a third-person perspective in which Crash moves into the screen. Certain levels that require him to flee from a rolling boulder reverse this perspective, while other levels are played from a traditional side-scrolling perspective. Crash is capable of moving in all directions; aside from moving left and right, he can move away from or toward the player, and the controls do not change with his position. His two primary forms of offense consist of jumping onto enemies and performing a spinning attack that kicks enemies off the screen. Kicked enemies can strike other enemies that are currently on-screen. Two levels involve Crash mounting and steering a wild boar that accelerates uncontrollably, requiring him to maneuver around obstacles and bypass enemies.

cards.heading: Fruit, checkpoints and TNT
cards.text: Scattered throughout each level are various types of crates that can be broken open by jumping on them, spinning into them, or knocking a kicked enemy into them. Most crates contain "Wumpa Fruit" that can grant Crash an extra life if 100 are collected. Some crates display an icon of what they contain. Crates displaying Aku Aku will grant Crash a floating Aku Aku mask that protects him from a single enemy or hazard. Collecting three masks consecutively grants Crash temporary invulnerability from all minor dangers. Crates marked with a "C" act as checkpoints where Crash can respawn after losing a life. Metallic crates marked with an exclamation point (!) cause an element of the surrounding environment to change if they are struck. Jumping on red TNT crates triggers a three-second timer that culminates in an explosion, while spinning into them causes an immediate detonation.

cards.heading: Streaming the world from the disc
cards.text: Spooling loaded new data as Crash moved forward or back through a level. Jason Rubin recalled Kelly Flock asking how many CD accesses finishing the game might require. Andy Gavin estimated roughly 120,000 offhand; Flock cited a 70,000 rating for the drive and continued supporting the project. The exchange illustrates the team's ambitions for a densely detailed world streamed from the disc.

main.title: Die Hard Trilogy
main.summary: Die Hard Trilogy is an action video game developed by Probe Entertainment, published by Fox Interactive and distributed by 20th Century Fox Home Entertainment in North America and Electronic Arts in Europe for the PlayStation, Sega Saturn and Microsoft Windows.

cards.heading: Three films, three kinds of action
cards.text: Die Hard Trilogy is an action video game developed by Probe Entertainment, published by Fox Interactive and distributed by 20th Century Fox Home Entertainment in North America and Electronic Arts in Europe for the PlayStation, Sega Saturn and Microsoft Windows. The game is based on the first three installments of the Die Hard series of action movies, with each film entry being represented through a different gameplay genre.

cards.heading: From the original trilogy to a sequel
cards.text: The game was well received and would eventually become a PlayStation Greatest Hits and PlayStation Platinum game. Die Hard Trilogy also inspired a sequel entitled Die Hard Trilogy 2: Viva Las Vegas. The sequel retained the three different playing styles but featured a spin-off storyline that was not connected to the movie series.

main.title: Wave Race 64
main.summary: Wave Race 64 is a 1996 racing video game developed and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64.

cards.text: Wave Race 64 is a 1996 racing video game developed and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64. It is the second entry in the Wave Race series following the 1992 Game Boy game Wave Race. Gameplay involves the player racing on a personal watercraft on a variety of courses while successfully manoeuvring the vehicle around various buoys. A multiplayer mode where two players can compete against each other on a chosen course is also included. The game supports the Controller Pak, which allows players to transfer saved data from one game cartridge to another. The game is presented in a letterboxed 14:9 aspect ratio.

Originally referred to as "F-Zero on water", the game was intended to feature high-speed boats with transforming capabilities, but these were ultimately replaced with Jet Skis as producer Shigeru Miyamoto felt that the game would not be differentiated enough from other titles on other systems. Wave Race 64 received acclaim from critics, who praised the game's satisfying controls and dynamic watery environments and considered as one of the best games ever made. The game is credited with helping Nintendo effectively make its paradigmatic leap from the 16-bit 2D graphics of the Super Nintendo Entertainment System to the Nintendo 64's 3D capabilities. It was re-released for the Wii and Wii U's Virtual Console in 2007 and 2016, respectively, and on the Nintendo Classics service in 2022. A sequel, Wave Race: Blue Storm, was released for the GameCube in 2001.

main.title: Wipeout 2097
main.summary: Wipeout 2097 (released as Wipeout XL in North America and Japan) is a 1996 racing video game developed and published by Psygnosis for the PlayStation.

cards.text: Wipeout 2097 (released as Wipeout XL in North America and Japan) is a 1996 racing video game developed and published by Psygnosis for the PlayStation. It is the second installment of the Wipeout series and a sequel to the original game, released the previous year. It was ported the following year to Microsoft Windows and the Sega Saturn, and later also to Amiga and Macintosh.

Whereas the original game introduced the F3600 anti-gravity racing league in 2052, Wipeout 2097 is set over four decades later and introduces the player to the much faster, more competitive, and more dangerous F5000 AG racing league. The game introduced a new damage interface and new weapons and tracks. The Sega Saturn version supported analogue control by using its 3D Control Pad, whereas the PlayStation version supported analogue control only through using the optional NeGcon twist controller.

Wipeout 2097 received critical acclaim upon release; reviewers praised the game for its dramatic improvements to the controls, graphics, and gameplay of the original Wipeout. The game featured a licensed electronic soundtrack featuring artists such as The Chemical Brothers and The Prodigy, an early example of modern licensed music being used in video games. Wipeout 2097 alongside its predecessor has since appeared on lists of the greatest games of all time by multiple publications.

main.title: Donkey Kong Country 3
main.summary: Donkey Kong Country 3: Dixie Kong's Double Trouble!  is a 1996 platform game developed by Rare and published by Nintendo for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES).

cards.heading: Dixie leads a new rescue
cards.text: Donkey Kong Country 3: Dixie Kong's Double Trouble!  is a 1996 platform game developed by Rare and published by Nintendo for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES). It is the third installment of the Donkey Kong Country series, and serves as a sequel to 1995's Donkey Kong Country 2: Diddy's Kong Quest. It was also re-released for the Game Boy Advance (GBA) in 2005. The game was made available to download on the Wii's Virtual Console service in 2007, as well as for the Wii U's Virtual Console in 2014.

cards.heading: Across the Northern Kremisphere
cards.text: The plot centers on Dixie Kong and her cousin, Kiddy Kong, in their attempts to save the captured Donkey Kong and Diddy Kong from the series' villain King K. Rool. The game is set in the "Northern Kremisphere", a fictionalized version of northern Europe and Canada. Dixie Kong's Double Trouble! utilises the same Silicon Graphics technology from its predecessors, which features the use of pre-rendered 3D imagery. The game received positive reviews upon release; critics praised the visuals and various aspects of gameplay, but noted a lack of innovation.

main.title: Command & Conquer: Red Alert
main.subtitle: Allies and Soviets in an alternate history
main.summary: Command & Conquer: Red Alert is a real-time strategy video game in the Command & Conquer franchise, developed and published by Westwood Studios in 1996.

cards.heading: Westwood revisits the origins of Command & Conquer
cards.text:
Command & Conquer: Red Alert is a real-time strategy video game in the Command & Conquer franchise, developed and published by Westwood Studios in 1996. The second game to bear the Command & Conquer title, Red Alert is the prequel to the original Command & Conquer of 1995, and takes place in the alternate early history of Command & Conquer when Allied Forces battle an aggressive Soviet Union for control over the European mainland.

It was initially available for PC (MS-DOS and Windows 95 versions included in one package) and was subsequently ported to PlayStation. The PlayStation version was also re-released as a download on the PlayStation Network for PlayStation Portable and PlayStation 3, but has since become delisted. On August 31, 2008, Electronic Arts, who acquired Westwood Studios in 1998, rendered Command & Conquer: Red Alert freeware.

cards.heading: Ore, power plants and captured factories
cards.text: Ore trucks bring resources to refineries, turning the map's deposits into credits for structures, troops, vehicles and repairs. Expanding that supply can strengthen an army, while denying ore to an opponent can slow theirs. A growing base also needs electricity: losing power can disable radar and Tesla Coils, making power plants important targets. Engineers offer another route into an enemy's capabilities. Capturing a damaged factory can allow a player to produce the opposing faction's vehicles, so a successful attack may gain a new tool as well as remove a threat.

cards.heading: Einstein changes history
cards.text: Red Alert imagines a different twentieth century. Einstein travels from 1946 to meet Hitler in 1924 and erases him from the timeline. The intervention prevents Nazi Germany's rise but leaves Stalin's Soviet Union free to expand across Asia and into Eastern Europe. Western European countries form the Allied Nations to resist. Their war supplies two campaigns built around rival armies, technologies and objectives, letting players approach this alternative conflict from either side.

cards.heading: Frank Klepacki and the 1997 expansions
cards.text:
The game's original score was composed by Frank Klepacki and was voted the best video game soundtrack of 1996 by PC Gamer and Gameslice magazines.

In 1997, two expansion packs for Red Alert were released for the PC, Command & Conquer: Red Alert: Counterstrike and Command & Conquer: Red Alert: The Aftermath. The expansion packs were designed by Westwood Studios with the "apprenticeship" of Intelligent Games, a London-based game developer. Much of the development on multiplayer maps was undertaken by players from the Compuserve Red Alert ladder. New units, missions, maps, and music were included in the expansions.
